title: Threat modelling with STRIDE
summary: Find the bugs before they are written: draw the data flow, mark the trust boundaries, walk STRIDE over each one, and fix a repudiation threat that is really an injection: forged log lines.

steps.title: Four questions and a drawing
body: Threat modelling is a design review with an attacker's hat on. It fits in a 45-minute meeting, and it answers four questions (Adam Shostack's framework):
1. **What are we working on?** Draw it: a data flow diagram with the people, processes, data stores and the arrows between them.
2. **What can go wrong?** Walk each arrow that crosses a **trust boundary** with STRIDE.
3. **What are we going to do about it?** A mitigation, an accepted risk, or a ticket for each threat.
4. **Did we do a good job?** Did the review find real problems? Do the tests check the mitigations?
Here is the Lamp Shop's link-preview feature, drawn as text:
```text
[Customer browser] --(1) GET /api/preview?url=...--> [Shop API] --(2) GET url--> [Any web server]
======== internet: trust boundary =========                   |
+--(3)--> [Reviews DB]
[Metadata 169.254.169.254]   (inside the cloud network)
Arrow (2) is where the design goes wrong: the shop makes requests **from inside** the network, to an address the customer chose. Nobody needs a scanner to see that once it is drawn.

steps.prompt: Each STRIDE threat breaks one security property. Match them.
pairs: **I**nformation disclosure: reading what you should not
**E**levation of privilege: doing what you may not

steps.title: STRIDE on one arrow
body: Take arrow (1), the customer's request to `/api/preview`, and ask each letter in turn:
| | Threat | Mitigation |
| S | A script on another site calls the preview with the user's cookie | it needs no session: make it anonymous, or check `Sec-Fetch-Site` |
| T | The `url` points at `http://169.254.169.254/` | allow-list of hosts, no redirects (task 12 of the live lab) |
| R | Nobody can tell who triggered a fetch | log the user and URL of every fetch |
| I | The preview returns the body of an internal page | return only the title, never the body |
| D | A URL to a 10 GB file, or one that never answers | timeout of 3 s, read at most 64 KB |
| E | Credentials from the metadata service act as the server's cloud role | IMDSv2, and a role with only the permissions it needs |
Not every letter finds something every time, and that is fine. The value is in asking all six on every boundary-crossing arrow, so the obvious-in-hindsight ones are not missed.

steps.prompt: Threats from a review of a password-reset feature. Which STRIDE letter is each?
items: Reset links are guessable sequential numbers, so anyone can reset anyone
The reset email is sent to the address given in the request, not the stored one
The `userId` in the reset form can be changed to another account's
The token in the link can be edited to extend its expiry
"No account with that email" tells an attacker who has an account
Reset tokens are written to the application log
A reset by a normal user can set `role=admin` in the same form
Resetting a password does not end the attacker's other sessions
steps.explain: Several fit two letters; pick the one the fix targets. Anything that lets you act **as** another user is spoofing; anything that lets you **change** what the server trusts is tampering.

steps.prompt: In a 45-minute threat model, which arrows deserve the most time?
options: Arrows that cross a trust boundary: from the internet, from a partner, from a less trusted service
Arrows between two functions in the same process
The arrows with the most traffic
steps.explain: Inside one process every call already shares the same trust. At a boundary, data from someone you do not control enters your code: that is where validation, authentication and authorization have to happen.

steps.title: Repudiation, and the forged log line
body: Audit logs are the answer to repudiation: "who refunded order 1003?". But a log line built by gluing strings is itself an injection target (CWE-117):
```csharp fragment
log.WriteLine($"user={user} action={action} target={target}");
A user who signs up with the name `alice\nuser=admin action=delete target=all` adds a second, fake line to the audit log:
```text
user=alice
user=admin action=delete target=all action=login target=web

Now the log blames the admin, and the investigation goes wrong. The fix is to **encode values** for the log's format: escape line breaks and quotes, quote values that contain spaces. Structured logging (`logger.LogInformation("Refund {OrderId} by {User}", id, user)` with a JSON sink) does this for you, which is one more reason to use it.

steps.title: An audit line that cannot be forged
prompt: Write `string AuditLine(string user, string action, string target)` that returns `user=<v> action=<v> target=<v>`, where each value `<v>` is:
- cut to its first **100** characters plus `...` when it is longer than 100;
- written **as it is** when it is not empty and only has ASCII letters, digits and `._@:/-`;

- otherwise wrapped in double quotes, with `\` written as `\\`, `"` as `\"`, carriage return as `\r`, line feed as `\n`, tab as `\t`, and any other control character as `\u` plus four hex digits (`\u0007`).
AuditLine("bob smith", "login", "")         ->  user="bob smith" action=login target=""
starter: string AuditLine(string user, string action, string target) =>
solution: string AuditLine(string user, string action, string target) =>
hints: Write a helper `string Value(string v)` and call it three times.
Decide first whether quoting is needed: `v.All(c => char.IsAsciiLetterOrDigit(c) || "._@:/-".Contains(c))`.
When quoting, build the result with a `StringBuilder` and a `switch` on each character; `char.IsControl(c)` catches the rest, and `$"\\u{(int)c:x4}"` formats one.
template: Dojo.Eq("a plain line", "user=alice action=refund target=order-1003", AuditLine("alice", "refund", "order-1003"));
Dojo.Eq("spaces are quoted, empty is \"\"", "user=\"bob smith\" action=login target=\"\"", AuditLine("bob smith", "login", ""));
Dojo.Check("a line feed in a value cannot start a new line", !forged.Contains('\n') && !forged.Contains('\r'), forged);
Dojo.Eq("...it is escaped inside quotes", "user=\"alice\\nuser=admin action=delete target=all\" action=login target=web", forged);
Dojo.Eq("quotes and backslashes are escaped", "user=\"say \\\"hi\\\" C:\\\\x\" action=a target=b", AuditLine("say \"hi\" C:\\x", "a", "b"));
Dojo.Eq("CR and tab are escaped", "user=\"a\\rb\\tc\" action=a target=b", AuditLine("a\rb\tc", "a", "b"));
Dojo.Eq("other control characters become \\u00XX", "user=\"bell\\u0007\" action=a target=b", AuditLine("bell\u0007", "a", "b"));
Dojo.Eq("emails and paths stay unquoted", "user=ada@shop.example action=export target=/reports/2026-11.csv", AuditLine("ada@shop.example", "export", "/reports/2026-11.csv"));
Dojo.Eq("a 150-character value is cut to 100 plus ...", "user=" + new string('a', 100) + "... action=a target=b", AuditLine(new string('a', 150), "a", "b"));
